# Block 6: Build your own agent in R {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/booktem_setup.R")
source("R/my_setup.R")
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(webexercises)
```

You build the two parts of an agent yourself, a conversation and a tool, then
run a complete agent on a real task and approve every step it takes. After
this, every control from Blocks 3 to 5 is something you can see in code.

*⏱ ~45 minutes · Start on `main`, Git pane clean, with your API key saved as
`AGENT_ANTHROPIC_KEY` ([setup](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#api-key)). Claude
Code is not used in this block.*

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## This block's files, and how it fits

You stay in your workshop repository, on `main`, straight after lunch. Claude
Code is set aside: you use an agent you can read line by line, and give it the
translation that the shipped `tests/test_translation.R` checks. Nothing later
in the day uses its output, so if time is short your instructor may run Task 2
on screen while you decide each approval in the chat.

| File | Where it comes from | Its job here |
|---|---|---|
| `data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv` | Shipped; used since Block 2 | The data the translation summarises |
| `scripts/functions/load_voles.R` | Shipped; used since Block 3 | Reads the data with fixed column types |
| `agent/mini_agent.R` | Shipped; first used here | The agent: four tools, its own permission rules and Manual-mode approvals |
| `tests/test_translation.R` | Shipped; first used here | Compares a tidyverse translation with the original base R code |
| `scripts/functions/summaries.R` | Written by your agent, with your approval, in Task 2 | The translation |
| A line in `docs/ai-log.md` | You, in Task 2 | The record |

**Before you start.** ellmer, the package that talks to Claude and runs the
loop, is pinned in your repository's `renv.lock`, so `renv::restore()`
installed it; never run `install.packages()` inside the project. Your key
comes from an Anthropic Console account, separate from a Claude subscription,
and lives in your user-level `.Renviron`, outside every repository. Every
request costs a little; Task 2 shows you how much the agent used.

The page follows the order of Hadley Wickham's explainer
[*What is an agent?*](https://substack.hadley.nz/p/what-is-an-agent): a
conversation, then a tool, then the loop. Joseph Barbier's talk *50 lines of
code to rebuild Claude Code in R* builds the same kind of agent; the version
here is our own.
:::


## Task 1: a conversation, then a tool

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Talk to a model, then give it a tool (8 minutes)
::::
::::{.task-container}

**Goal:** see what one request to a model is, and what a tool request is, so
that nothing your agent does in Task 2 is a surprise.

**1. Have a conversation.** In the R console:

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(ellmer)

key <- function() Sys.getenv("AGENT_ANTHROPIC_KEY")
chat <- chat_anthropic(model = "claude-sonnet-5-5", credentials = key)
chat$chat("Tell me a joke about R.")
chat$chat("Explain why it is funny, in one sentence.")
chat
```

Printing `chat` shows the conversation as `r glossary("turn", "turns")`. The
second question works only because ellmer sends the **whole conversation so
far** with each request: the model keeps nothing between requests. That is the
[context window](11-AI-programming-integrated.qmd) from Block 1, and why a long
conversation costs more per question.

**2. Give it a tool.** A tool is an R function the model may ask you to run:

```{r}
#| eval: false
today <- tool(
  function() format(Sys.Date()),
  name = "today",
  description = "Get today's date."
)

chat <- chat_anthropic(model = "claude-sonnet-5-5", credentials = key)
chat$register_tool(today)
chat$chat("How many days until 25 December?")
chat
```

The model sees only the tool's name and description. Its first reply is a
request, "call `today`"; ellmer runs `today()` **on your computer** and sends
the result back; then the model answers. That is two
`r glossary("request", "requests")` for one question.

**You are done when** you can point, in the printed `chat`, to the tool
request and to the tool result, and say which of them ran on your computer.

**If it goes wrong:** if the first `chat$chat()` reports a missing or invalid
key, check `Sys.getenv("AGENT_ANTHROPIC_KEY") != ""`, and restart R after
editing `.Renviron`.

::::
:::


## The loop

An `r glossary("agent")` repeats that exchange: the harness sends the
conversation, runs any tool the model asks for, adds the result, and sends it
all again, until a reply asks for no tool. Every control in this course acts on
one of three facts:

- **The model only asks.** The harness runs each tool on your computer, so
  that is where Manual mode asks you, a deny rule refuses, and a hook inspects.
- **Results go back to the model.** A tool that reads a data file sends that
  data to the provider: [Block 3's disclosure route](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd).
- **The model decides when to stop.** It can loop longer than you expect,
  which is why a real harness has limits and a stop key.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## How it works: the loop with no model at all

This code runs without an API key. It replaces the model with a pretend one
that follows a script; each pass of `repeat` is one request.

```{r}
# the tools, as plain R functions
tools <- list(
  n_rows = function(name) {
    nrow(get(name, envir = as.environment("package:datasets")))
  }
)

# a pretend model: asks for a tool until it has two results, then answers
pretend_model <- function(turns) {
  results <- Filter(function(t) t$role == "tool result", turns)
  if (length(results) == 0) {
    list(role = "assistant", tool = "n_rows", args = list(name = "mtcars"))
  } else if (length(results) == 1) {
    list(role = "assistant", tool = "n_rows", args = list(name = "iris"))
  } else {
    list(role = "assistant",
         text = paste("iris has", results[[2]]$text, "rows and mtcars has",
                      results[[1]]$text, "so iris has more."))
  }
}

# the harness: send the conversation, run any tool asked for, repeat
question <- "Which has more rows, mtcars or iris?"
turns <- list(list(role = "user", text = question))
repeat {
  reply <- pretend_model(turns)
  turns <- c(turns, list(reply))
  if (is.null(reply$tool)) break # no tool asked for: this is the answer
  result <- do.call(tools[[reply$tool]], reply$args)
  turns <- c(turns, list(list(role = "tool result", text = result)))
}

for (t in turns) {
  what <- if (is.null(t$tool)) t$text else
    paste0("call ", t$tool, "(", t$args, ")")
  cat(sprintf("%-12s %s\n", t$role, what))
}
```

`do.call()` is the only line that does anything to your computer: that is
where Manual mode, deny rules and hooks act. In the real API the tool result
goes back inside a user turn; ellmer does that for you.
:::


## Your agent: `agent/mini_agent.R`

Your repository ships a complete agent built from the same parts, about 120
lines. Your instructor walks through it; each part matches something from this
morning:

- **Four tools.** `list_files()` and `read_file()` look around; `write_file()`
  and `run_r()` change things.
- **`inside_project()` is its deny rule.** It may read inside the project,
  except raw data and credentials files, and write **only under `scripts/`**,
  so it cannot edit its checks in `tests/` or its own rules in `agent/`.
- **`ask_first()` is Manual mode.** Reads go straight through; every write and
  every run is shown to you first, and refused unless you choose **Yes**.
- **The system prompt is its instruction file.** It is not given your
  `AGENTS.md` (it could still open the file, like any other), and like
  `AGENTS.md` its prompt is only a request.

`run_r()` shows the gap Block 5 found: R code can write anywhere, `data/raw/`
included, and read anything you can, your `.Renviron` included. Only your
approval stands in the way, which is why you read the code before you choose
**Yes**; afterwards the Git pane shows any change.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Reference: the full `agent/mini_agent.R`

```{r, eval = FALSE, file = here::here("_instructor", "template-files", "agent", "mini_agent.R")}
```

`list_files()` lists one folder and at most 100 names, and `read_file()`
returns at most 300 lines: a recursive listing would include every package in
`renv/`, and all of it would be sent to the model. An error in a tool does not
stop the agent: ellmer sends the error message back to the model, which can
try something else. `run_r()` uses a fresh R session (`callr::r()`), so it
cannot change the objects in yours, and only the first 60 lines of its output
go back to the model.
:::


## Task 2: run your agent

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Run your agent (20 minutes)
::::
::::{.task-container}

**Goal:** watch your own agent write, test and fix a translation while you
approve every write and run, so that you see exactly where Manual mode and a
deny rule act.

**Start state:** `main`, Git pane clean, R's working directory at the
repository's root (as it is when you open the project).

**1. Load the agent.** Nothing is sent to the model yet:

```{r}
#| eval: false
source(here::here("agent", "mini_agent.R"))
```

**2. Give it the task.** The original base R code is `legacy_rate_summary()`
in `tests/test_translation.R`, which also checks the translation:

```{r}
#| eval: false
chat$chat(paste(
  "Write a function summarise_rate_tidy(data) in scripts/functions/summaries.R",
  "whose output matches legacy_rate_summary() in tests/test_translation.R.",
  "Use dplyr and the native pipe; it must work in a fresh R session.",
  "Write only that file, and no tests. Then run",
  "testthat::test_file('tests/test_translation.R') with run_r, and fix the",
  "function until the test passes."
))
```

**3. Decide each request.** Reads run without asking. For a `write_file` or
`run_r` request, read what it prints and choose **Yes** only for a write to
`scripts/functions/summaries.R` or a run of the test. **Refuse the first test
run on purpose:** the agent stops and explains. Then let it continue:

```{r}
#| eval: false
chat$chat("Go ahead and run the test.")
```

**4. Look inside.**

```{r}
#| eval: false
chat               # every turn: your prompt, its tool requests, the results
count_requests()   # how many requests it sent to the model
chat$get_tokens()  # the tokens it sent and received
```

**5. Check its work yourself.** The agent's "the test passes" is a claim. Read
the diff of `scripts/functions/summaries.R` in the Git pane, then restart R
(*Session → Restart R*) and run:

```{r}
#| eval: false
testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests"))
```

**6. Record and commit.** Add a line to `docs/ai-log.md` with today's date,
for example
`2026-10-22; mini agent (ellmer, claude-sonnet-5-5); translated the rate summary to tidyverse; kept after reading the diff and running the tests`,
then commit `summaries.R` and the log.

`r hide("Did your agent notice the missing value?")`

`aggregate()` with a formula silently drops the animal whose
`metabolic_rate_post` is missing, so the original's mean and count leave it
out. A literal tidyverse translation keeps it: an `NA` mean and a count one
too high. The test compares against the original, so the agent had to match
that behaviour, and if it read the test it probably did so without comment.
The test checks "the same as the original", not "correct": Block 8 returns to
that difference.

`r unhide()`

**You are done when** `test_translation.R` passes in your own run, the Git
pane showed only `summaries.R` and your log changed, you can say how many
requests and tokens the task took, and both are committed.

**If it goes wrong:**

- **The agent loops or goes off course:** answer **No**, then steer it with
  `chat$chat("…")`, or `source()` the file again to start a new conversation.
- **A refused path you expected to work:** check `getwd()` is the
  repository's root.
- **An unwanted change:** **Revert** it in the Git pane.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## What did it cost?

`chat$get_cost()` turns the tokens into money when ellmer knows the model's
price. If it shows `NA`, run `ellmer::models_update_prices()` once to refresh
ellmer's price list, or multiply the tokens from `chat$get_tokens()` by the
prices on Anthropic's pricing page. `claude-opus-5-5`, set at the top of
`mini_agent.R`, is a larger model at a higher price per token.
:::

::::
:::


## What Claude Code adds

| Your mini agent | Claude Code |
|---|---|
| `ask_first()` and `tool_reject()` | Manual mode (`default`) and the other permission modes |
| `inside_project()`: writes only under `scripts/` | Deny rules in `.claude/settings.json`, such as `Edit(/data/raw/**)` |
| The system prompt | `AGENTS.md`, read at the start of each session |
| `run_r()` in a fresh R session | Commands it runs in the Terminal; you check results in a fresh R session |
| `chat`, `count_requests()`, `chat$get_tokens()` | The conversation itself, and the model shown in Claude Code |
| Git | Git |

Claude Code adds plan mode, hooks, skills, compaction of long conversations,
many more tools and far more checks around each one. Building the small
version is a way to understand the big one, not a reason to use it for real
work. In Block 7 you hand Claude Code a much bigger job under the same
controls.


:::{.callout-note}
## Check · Reproduce · Record

- **You can now:** explain an agent as a model, a harness and tools in a loop,
  and run one in R, **trusted because** you can read every line that touches
  your files, and a test you did not write decides whether its change is
  right.
- **Check:** every write and every run is shown to you before it happens; the
  Git pane shows what changed; the test runs in a fresh R session.
- **Reproduce:** `run_r()` runs in a fresh R session, so the agent's checks do
  not depend on what is loaded in yours.
- **Record:** `chat` holds the full record of what was sent and received; your
  AI-use log records the tool, the model and what you kept.
:::


## Check your understanding

**In an agent built with ellmer, who runs a tool's R function?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "The model, on Anthropic's servers",
  answer = "The harness (ellmer), on your computer, after the model asks for it",
  "Nobody: the model predicts what the function would return",
  "RStudio, in a separate window"
))`

**True or false: when an agent's tool reads a file, the file's contents are sent to the model provider.** `r torf(TRUE)`

**`inside_project()` lets the agent write only under `scripts/`. Which tool call could still change a raw data file?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "read_file('data/raw/voles_raw.csv')",
  "write_file('data/raw/voles_raw.csv', '...')",
  answer = "run_r() with code that writes to data/raw/",
  "list_files('data/raw')"
))`


## Going further (not covered live)

This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if
it is useful to you.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Add a `run_tests` tool

Replace general-purpose `run_r()` for checking with a tool that can only run
the project's tests, `function() testthat::test_dir("tests")` run through
`callr::r()`. A narrow tool needs less approval than a general one: you might
let it through without asking, and keep asking for `run_r()`.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## A restricted mode

Change `ask_first()` so it asks before every call, reads included. You then
see every file the agent wants to read before it is sent to the provider,
which is the habit Block 3 recommends near confidential data.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Packages that do more

- [btw](https://posit-dev.github.io/btw/) gives ellmer agents ready-made tools
  for R: package documentation, your live session's objects and your project's
  files.
- [mcptools](https://posit-dev.github.io/mcptools/) connects R to the Model
  Context Protocol, so R functions can be tools for other assistants, including
  Claude Code.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Another provider

ellmer has a `chat_*()` function for each provider it supports, and the tools
and loop stay the same. Tool calling can be much less reliable with small local
models, so start with a hosted model.
:::
